p: And that includes course materials and everything else, or—
I think that's the total course—
[interposing] Okay.
cost, but if there's something additional, I'll correct that, but I believe it's a total of $25.
Please describe the practical examination component of the course. What does this exam consist of, and who conducts it?

The practical exam is conducted by an equine veterinarian with a horse. And the driver needs to demonstrate, for example, the proper fitting of the bridle and the harness, proper hitching and unhitching, managing and control of the horse.

The committee has heard from many animal sanctuaries across the country that have stated they are willing to accept the horses in the event that the industry is phased out. Is DOHMH equipped to coordinate with city agencies, sanctuaries, and animal welfare organizations to transition horses to safe and caring homes, and to ensure that none are sold or disposed of in a manner that leads to slaughter or mistreatment?

So the bill would require the Health Department to collect information about sanctuaries and similar organizations and people, and to provide that information to the owners and then to collect certifications from the owners about the disposition of their horse. We are reviewing the bill, so we don't have exactly the details for how we would

implement that, but we would be prepared to implement should the bill pass.
That’s what I'm asking you, if you're prepared and do you need– do you need other resources to facilitate that?
We haven't fully evaluated the requirements of the bill. We are still reviewing.
How many staff positions does DOHMH dedicate to carriage horses?

So we have six inspectors who work on this industry but also other animal-related industries. And then we have, you know, program leads, administrative staff, and then equine veterinarians on contract.
If the council enacts Intro 943, does DOHMH have a plan to transition those staff?
So these staff work on a number of different programs, and so there's no concern about having them— there will be other work for them to do.

Please describe how DOHMH communicates and works with DCWP to enforce

local laws governing the carriage horse industry. Is there a multi-agency team that regularly coordinates on enforcement, trainings, and emergency response?
We do communicate regularly with the many agencies that have a role in oversight of the industry.

I would add to that, I know I've personally participated in a citywide task force that is essential— that is focused on Central Park and issues as it relates to particularly horse-drawn carriages. That also– work happens in coordination with local stakeholders as well.
Are any other agencies such as Parks and NYPD involved in this process?
Yes, they are. They both are.

The Rental Horse Advisory Board is required to advise the Commission on regulations affecting the health, safety, and welfare of carriage horses and the public. Has the Advisory Board met in recent years, and if so, what

recommendations or actions has it taken to improve passenger safety?

So the Advisory Board is established in the local law. It has been constituted. There isn't a formal role for the Health Department beyond once the Health Commissioner has designated the members. So we are aware of meetings, but we don't have a role in those meetings, so I can't speak to really their meeting schedule. There have— they have not delivered recommendations to the Commissioner, the Health Commissioner in many, many years.

The Rental Horse Advisory Board is required to advise the Commissioner on regulations affecting the health, safety, and welfare of carriage horses in the public. What? Oh, I did? I'm sorry. Oh yeah, sorry about that. Does the agency envision any potential challenges should Intro 943 be enacted?

We are continuing to review the bill, but as you have heard from both Deputy Commissioner Ortiz and myself, the administration supports the bill with some interest

in continuing to discuss some of the provisions with the council.
Okay, I'm going to ask some questions for you, Carlos. How many active carriage owner licenses exist currently? Our research shows the number at 52.
There are 68 carriage licenses currently, Chair.
Alright. How many carriages are currently in operation?
I'm not sure how much are operating throughout the day, but there's 68 that are authorized to work.
Is that number different than the number of owner licenses?
68 should correspond to the— it is the owner license.
Okay. But does that differ from what's in operation? That's what I'm asking.

So there are 68 licenses that relate to the carriage. Those are the owner licenses. There are 208 licenses for drivers. I wouldn't say every driver is operating

every day. The carriages, I think it fluctuates based on what the owner wants to put out that day.
What is the average value of a carriage owner license?

Now we looked over the bills of sales. I think on average, there's— over the many years, there's maybe $70,000 approximately. I think that that could fluctuate. It could be— there could be different negotiating terms in each contract. So, it's something we can continue to evaluate with the council.
Okay. Are owner licenses transferable? If so, how?

They are transferable. Right now there's a cap on the category that I think was instituted 10 or so years ago. It requires an agreement between the previous owner and then the new one and the notification to the agency as well.
What happens to an owner license if it expires? Can it be renewed?

Yes, if– I believe we were able to issue up to the cap, which is

68. So if there's an expiration, we'd be able to issue a license.
Can expired licenses be recovered in any way?

There's typically— once there's a– there’s typically a grace period we provide after an expiration to allow a business to come back in and renew. This is applicable to all of our categories. The grace period is 59 days. If you're coming back for a license after the 59-day period, generally you're going to have to get a new license.
Alright, thank you. Council Member Marte.
Thank you, Chair. Last year the Department of Health ordered an independent veterinarian to inspect the stables and test the horses. What was the process in choosing that veterinarian?

In late 2025, the Health Department undertook a pilot initiative to conduct exams, clinical exams, as part of our stable inspection. So we put out a solicitation broadly to sending it to equine

veterinarians we could identify in New York State and the surrounding states. We- there was one response.
Okay. And so you say that this veterinarian was completely independent from the administration, willing to do the work with an independent mindset?
The veterinarian who responded to the solicitation met the requirements of the solicitation, which was that they were not– we wanted someone who was not engaged already in the industry.
And can you elaborate on the investigation and the findings of the veterinarian?

The veterinarian did an assessment of 12 horses, and following the same– the administrative code sets out really a lot of the details, the details for the assessment that a veterinarian needs to do of the horse to show that the horse is fit to work in the industry. And so this veterinarian was doing that same assessment with the caveat that it— these assessments were conducted in the stable. So there were some limitations, because of that environment.
And is 12 an average amount of inspection of horses that typically happen, or is that far below the average if someone were to go and investigate fully the stables and the horses?
The pilot program that we did at the end of 2025 looked at— was completed for 12 horses.
Okay. I have a question for Mr. Ortiz. Would the administration be open to a shorter phase-out period if we included worker protections that will allow workers to find new employment sooner?

I think we would have to discuss. I'm certainly encouraged by the perspective of ensuring that we have pathways for workers. I think on balance we'd have to review the bill in totality to see if a shorter phase-out is accomplished— it was something we can accomplish. But I think we're very much open to ideas right now on the table for this.
One final question. I'll come back. Thank you, Chair.
Ask the one final question, but we're trying to keep on time here because we have a lot of people testifying.
I resp— I don't need to ask this question.
You sure?
I respect that.

Okay. Alright. Council member– before I do that, I just want to say one thing. You know, I'm a big fan of– well, two things. One is we've been joined by Council Member Hanif. The other is that I'm a big fan of DOHMH, but I'm disappointed at the data questions that we asked that we didn't get answers to, because those questions were submitted to you guys beforehand. So I just want to make mention of that. I'm going to ask Councilmember Epstein to ask questions.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Speaker. Can I just ask about the six staff? You said they are working in other industries. What percentage of their time are dealing with horse issues for the six staff?
I don't have a percentage of time. I would estimate what's probably equivalent to one

One FTE for all the horses? Great. Thank you very much. Carlos, can I talk about the transitions? You flagged the concerns about making sure there's sufficient worker protections in this transition. When you say that, when you say worker protections, do you mean helping them transition to a new industry or transition into a related industry just without the horses?

I think it's really about securing outcomes for the workers. So I think a transition into employment, I think, is something that we'd be interested in exploring. I know it's come up in our conversations with labor partners. I know the bill already contemplates workforce development, for example.
Right.
So I think that's what we're referring to.

So, workforce development, but you– they could be in this industry

like tourism or within a separate industry? Is that what you're flagging?

I think– well, I think part of that conversation needs to happen with workers as well in terms of what industries they wanna be moving into. And, yeah, I think that's an important question for them. I think we are certainly open to facilitating what outcomes they need.

And what is your timeline for that? Just so— obviously this is, you know, a pressing issue. Unfortunately, we've already just had a loss of life. So are you thinking that conversations are going to be happening in the next couple of weeks?
I think the conversations are already happening on this, and I think the timeline will have to align with the prospective timeline for this bill to engage in legislative process.
Alright, thank you very much, and thank you, Chair.
Okay.

I do– Chair, I just want to clarify my comment on the work on our

staff was about our health inspectors. There are other staff who work in the industry– who work on this industry as well, reviewing documentation, and as I mentioned, our equine veterinarians.
Yeah, one full-time equivalent of person going out for a health—
[interposing] For the health inspector. I just want to make sure that was clear.
For the health inspector, exactly.
Thank you.
Thank you. Helpful. Thank you. Council Member Wilson?

Thank you, Chair, and thank you for your testimony. So I live across the street from the stables in Hell's Kitchen. I— they— the stables are called— are homed in District 3. So I see the horses quite a bit walking to and from the park every morning. And, you know, my partner is a lifelong equestrian, so horse care is like very important to me and my family. So I have a couple of questions about the transition for the

horses. I respect that you said you're still putting this together, but you mentioned in your testimony that you would collect information about the sanctuaries or I guess retirement farms, that these horses would go to. So, approximately how long will that process take? And once that's given to the drivers, will that be the list of who they can go to, or would they be allowed to find other homes for the horses?

So the bill specifies the— gives the department direction for information to collect and to provide to the owners. We are still looking at that, and should the bill pass, which as you know we support with caveats, we would be refining that process.

So would there be any— once the horse is there, is thought to how— would there be any follow-up at the sanctuaries or retirement homes, retirement farms, to ensure that they are indeed being taken care of?
So I think we're continuing to review the bill to assess that.

Okay. I guess my point is that, you know, it's very nice to say that

they, you know, they'll be transitioned and sent to a retirement farm or sanctuary, but oftentimes there's more to it than that for the well-being of the horses. The transition from one environment to another can be disruptive, and we'd want to just make sure that they are actually being taken care for, and it's not just a line written on the page, but something the city continues to follow up on to ensure.

I think that point is well taken, Council Member. And we're also encouraged that our colleagues in the Mayor's Office on Animal Welfare have already received outreach from equestrian sanctuaries to engage in this work. But I think, even as we phase out, it'll have to be an interdisciplinary and multi-agency effort and ensuring, for example, that that office is involved and running checks on this is important too.
Okay, thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much. Council Member Morano.

Thank you, Chair, for your willingness to hold this hearing. I know

it's been a long time coming. I also want to thank the Speaker for her leadership on this issue. I know it takes a lot of courage to be the first sitting Speaker to take this particular position on this issue. But aside from taking a position that I happen to agree with, I want to commend you for the really responsible way in which you're addressing concerns about job loss and things of that nature and not seeking to demagogue the issue at all. And it's a— it's a tough thing to do, and I want to thank you for your leadership on that. I'd also be remiss if I didn't mention the leadership of former Councilman Holden. And had we acted on this legislation when he was in the council, perhaps a young man would still be alive today. That being said, thank you, Deputy Commissioner, for your testimony. And to the extent that you need Mr. Ortiz to assist you with my questions, please just have him do so. I want to start with something in your testimony that really jumped out at me. You tell us the health department reviews health certificates. You check that horses are examined every four to eight months. You review furlough records. You make periodic observations. You monitor you issue weather-related suspensions, and

you actually conduct the training course that aspiring carriage drivers must complete. That's a lot of regulation, and yet an 18-year-old young man is dead. So I want to ask you a question that I don't mean rhetorically at all. At what point does a regulator have an obligation to say, well, we've regulated this activity as much as we reasonably can, and the inherent risk remains?
So I would say that the Health Department is exercising the authority that the City Council has given to us. And my understanding is that is— your question is why we are here today.

Right. And because I keep hearing proposals for another inspection, another training requirement, another rule, another layer of enforcement. I'm wondering, can you identify for me a regulation that would eliminate a horse's instinct to bolt when frightened?

I think– I think, Councilmember, this is— I would say this is probably the third administration I've worked in now where we as an administration are supportive of winding down this industry. And I think your point is

well taken that, you know, we could be working on the margins to try and address what's happening in the industry to find short-term solutions, but ultimately we as administration are supportive of a long-term solution that protects the conditions of workers, the horses, and New Yorkers.

Let me ask you something else, and I'll be considerate of everyone else's time. If there were no horse-drawn carriage industry in New York City today, and someone came to your department with a proposal to create one, to place large prey animals in one of the most heavily visited urban parks in the world, attach open passenger carriages to them, and sell rides to to the public, knowing everything your department knows today, would the health department recommend that the city approve that new industry?
It is– you're in the— what you imply is well taken, and I think as my colleague is saying, that is why we are here today.
Thanks very much.
Thank you very much, Council Member Morano. Next is Council Member Narcisse.

Thank you, Chair, and first foremost, thank you, Madam Speaker, and the family. I feel you. Thank you so much for being here, being present, and using the time to let us know what's going on with you. It's difficult time, and as a mother of four, I can feel you sitting here. Now, is it difficult for me to even— Let me go to the question. This is a— the– you know, listening to you is just in my head. What is the administration's plan for the horses themselves, rehoming, sanctuaries, placement oversight, and who is financially responsible for that transition? That's one. The bill that we have here in our hands focus on the licensing of the drivers. What happens to the stable— I mean, the stable hands and other workers– Local 100 and the union have said the industry supports. Are they eligible for any of this transition benefits? Third, what specific industries or role is DCWP targeting for placement? Is this a real pipeline into union jobs or a genetic resume workshop program? Do you know?

I'll start with the questions about the horses, and the bill is quite detailed, directing the health department to collect information about where the horses might go and to provide that information to the owners and then requiring that the owners certify to the disposition of the horses and provide that certification to the Health department. We are still reviewing those provisions and to determine exactly how we would do that should the bill pass. And as Deputy Commissioner Ortiz mentioned, and I agree, we would work very closely with the Mayor's Office of Animal Welfare on that.

And I would add, Council Member, you know, the bill already describes a workforce development program for horse-drawn carriage drivers and other workers engaged in the business of operating such horse-drawn cabs. To me, that— I mean, I'm encouraged that the council has already drafted or is keeping these workers in mind, both the drivers and the stablehands. I think we want to make sure that that is preserved throughout a final version of the bill

in whichever mechanism we decide to be able to support the workers.
Tough one. What could have done here in this situation to prevent the death of this young man?
You know, as the Speaker eloquently articulated, this was preventable. The council has set out a law that clearly says that a horse must be attended to, cannot be left unattended.
And one life is too many. Thank you so much. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much. Council Member Brewer?

Thank you very much. A couple of questions. One is just in terms of how does Health Department and NYPD, how do they communicate? You said that when there is a situation where the Health Department has perhaps given some summonses, but the NYPD does the actual violations depending on the situation. How does that communication take place?

We're in regular communication with NYPD, particularly on days

days like today and yesterday where we know it's— we're most likely going to meet those reach those weather thresholds, those temperature and humidity thresholds. So it is routine. What I— what I meant to say about the summonses is that we are not necessarily at the HAC stands at the time that those suspensions occur. So in order to provide the Chair with full information about violations, I wanted to be able to get that to talk to NYPD first.
Okay, so you basically back and forth with email situations?
Emails, phone calls, you know, not only during the business day, off hours, weekends. It is a regular communication.
Okay, go ahead.
I’ll also add– I'm sorry, Council Member.
Go ahead, Carlos.

I would just add to the processes of having this joint task force that we've had centralized in Central Park. The DCWP has also facilitated training that we provide Central Park, and Parks Enforcement Patrol as well on what

issues they need to look out for as they conduct their on-street or in-park enforcement.

Okay, thank you. Other cities— in the briefing paper talks about Philly and other places. My issue is workers. In some cases they've had job fairs. They're much smaller numbers. I think it were 10 people who actually— or Chicago was even fewer. But have you looked to see what worker programs have been effective in other cities, or they're too small to even consider? Because you have obviously many more.

We— thus far, the DCWP has not looked into other worker programs. I know we've had initial conversations with our colleagues, such as at the Mayor's Office of Talent Workforce Development that will have feedback on how to build a sustainable program. But I think if there's lessons to be learned from other municipalities about how they transitioned out, we are certainly open to taking that feedback.

I mean, obviously the briefing paper had some— you could get the same, but there were some ideas there. I've been on this bill– I've been in the City Council, 2002, a long

time. And I've been on this bill except when there was an electric car. I am absolutely opposed to any car more in Central Park. I'm the author of the bill to get them out. So I want to make sure that the administration is not talking about electric cars or anything like it in terms of this discussion.
I, thus far, have had no conversations on my end related to electric cars.
Health Department?
Nor have I, and I did not see that in the bill.

Okay. I know it's not in the bill. I want to make sure nobody pops up with it. Okay, and then the other— so we got workers, horses, jobs, and tourists. And so I am supportive of tourists using pedicabs. Is that something that you support? Have you had any thoughts about it? Obviously, we have legislation that hasn't been finalized, but we're thinking about it. Is that something that you think could address the need for tourists? I take pedicabs. You should see me, I know how to do it. But I know how to organize how much I

pay. So I'm just wondering what you're thinking about tourism for the future in Central Park.

I think pedicabs will still be an ongoing activity that's happening in Central Park. You know, I did notice, a few months back, I think that the Midtown Community Justice Center released a report of recommendations as it relates to the pedicab industry. I think many of the recommendations in there were well taken, and certainly if we're looking to strengthen or improve the pedicab industry as a substitute in the future, DCWP will be ready to engage in that conversation too.
Alright. I had a lot to do with that report, so I appreciate it. Thank you.
Thank you very much. Council Member Hanif?

Thank you, Chair. I just want to begin by talking to the Mahajan family. Thank you for being here. I'm so sorry for your loss, and thank you for trusting the council with Romanch's story. I'm thinking of you and your family, and passing this piece of legislation is the

most important thing that must come out of today's hearing, and we're grateful that the speaker and our mayor are supportive. I'd like to know, what oversight does DOHMH currently have over the health and welfare of carriage horses, and what are the limits of that authority? And if you could keep it brief. It's a big question.

The [inaudible] is quite specific in the role— in setting out the role of the health department and what we can require from the industry. So there is– as I mentioned in my testimony, that's highlighting some of the key areas. The horse owners are required to have veterinary exams every four to eight months and to submit certifications of those exams to us. We are reviewing those. They are required to submit documentation showing proof of vacation furlough five weeks a year at a place where there is a pasture opportunity for turnout. The license is renewable. So there's all of those things that we are checking.
Got it. And then is there a standardized criteria for determining when a horse is not fit?
There— we have a form. We have a certification form that a veterinarian licensed in New York State signs off on. And our equine veterinarian reviews those.
How frequently are vets checking horses' health?
So the owners' vets have—
[interposing] Is there a DOHMH vet and then an owner's vet? And what's the frequency?

So the Administrative Code requires a veterinarian check every four to eight months. The owners have veterinarians who check their horses. We have veterinarians who over— who review those certifications. A veterinarian would also— we also, as I noted earlier, when we have reason to think that there's need for an assessment of a horse because of our observation or something referred to us by NYPD or we are observing based on a complaint, we will also direct the owner to have the veterinarian, its veterinarian, assess the horse.
And are you able to share how many violations DOHMH issued over the last five years for non-compliance or adherence to the many forms and check-ins?

I have the— I have 2023 through April 2026. So for lacking a record of a medical exam or the exam not within the time frame, we've issued 17 summonses. Missing proof of five weeks of furlough, we have 12.
I'll come back for a second round.
Okay, thank you. Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chair. A question regarding the mayor's executive order. Let me get to that. Mayor Eric Adams issued Executive Order 56 in September 2025 directing your agency, that's DCWP, to identify alternative employment for carriage workers. Between September 2025 and today, were any workers contacted, and how many were offered services, and how many were placed in new jobs? Please answer that.
